title: Stove
description: Device used to generate heat or to cook
wiki_lead:
A stove or range is an appliance or construction that generates heat inside or atop the device using an energy source. They differ from ovens, since ovens keep their heat in closed chambers, while stoves typically allow their heat to flow outwards.
Stoves are used for cooking or indoor heating, traditionally both. Stoves contain and concentrate heat for better efficiency than a firepit or hearth. Stoves can be powered with many fuels, such as wood, coal, natural gas, propane, oil, kerosine, and electricity. Other than ovens, stoves are the most common and traditional fixtures for applying heat to food for cooking.
Traditionally, stoves were built from stones, clay, rammed-earth, or bricks. In modern times, stoves made of Cast-iron, steel, and glass tops are common. Brick stoves are still common in outdoor settings, such as parks and backyards. Despite being firepits, more sophisticated dug-out structures with a designated fire chamber and designated cooking part (such as the dakota fire hole) can arguably be considered a stove that uses the earth as its body.
Modern cooking stoves often double as stoves and ovens. Developed nations today typically use electric-stoves or gas-stoves for cooking. Developing nations and rural areas typically still use wood-fire stoves or firepits for cooking meals and heating the home.
Electric and Magnetic-induction stoves are the popular choice in home kitchens, because their energy levels can be controlled exactly, and do not involve a flame, keeping the indoor air clean, preventing carbon-monoxide buildup, and greatly reducing the chances of a house fire; as well as being more energy efficient, which lowers costs long term. Gas-stoves also have a risk of gas leaks, either from a leaking gas line, or someone forgetting to turn the dial to 'off' after putting out the flames.
Propane or natural-gas stoves are more common in institutional kitchens and restaurants, because gas-stoves offer instant heat, more intense heat, and long-term durability, while still offering some heat-control. These attributes are ideal for situations where speed, bulk-efficiency, and heavy usage are needed. 
Concerns about air pollution have fostered efforts to improve stove design, and replace old stoves with better alternatives. Pellet stoves, for instance, are a type of clean-burning stove. Air-tight stoves, another type, burn their fuel more completely than conventional ones and so reduce the amount of the combustion by-products. Rocket Stoves are a recently invented stove type, that are engineered for the complete-combustion of wood, which is helpful for people in developing countries who rely on wood fires for cooking. Another method of reducing air pollution is through the addition of a device to clean the exhaust gas, such as a filter or afterburner. Research and development on safer and lower-emission stoves is continuously evolving.

Etymology

Old English had a word stofa, meaning a hot-air bath or sweating room. However, this usage did not survive, and the word was taken newly from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch in the 15th or 16th century, later meaning any room heated with a furnace. By the 17th century it had come to mean a heated box such as an oven, and by the 18th century could mean an open fireplace.


History


Versions prior
Cooking was performed over an open fire since nearly two million years ago. It is uncertain how fires were started at these times; some hypotheses include the removal of burning branches from wildfires, spark generation through hitting rocks, or accidental lighting through the chipping of stone tools. During the Paleolithic era, approximately 200,000 to 40,000 years ago, primitive hearths were constructed, with stones arranged in a circle shape. Human homes centered around these hearths for warmth and food. grok_lead: A stove is an enclosed appliance that generates heat through the controlled combustion of fuel such as wood, coal, gas, or electricity, primarily for cooking food or warming interiors, offering greater efficiency, safety, and smoke management than open fires by containing flames and channeling exhaust via flues or chimneys. Originating as simple cast-iron heating devices in late 15th-century Europe, such as the Dutch jamb stove, early models focused on room warming before evolving into dedicated cooking ranges in the 18th century with inventions like the French stew stove of 1735 and Benjamin Franklin's 1742 Pennsylvania fireplace, which improved heat circulation through air ducts. Subsequent advancements shifted to coal, natural gas, and electric variants, enabling precise temperature regulation and reducing reliance on manual fuel tending, thereby transforming domestic energy use and culinary practices worldwide. These developments stemmed from empirical needs for better combustion and heat transfer, as inefficient open-hearth methods wasted up to 90% of fuel energy, while enclosed designs captured more thermal output for practical ends.
